about.title: Highland Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Medical malpractice cases in San Bernardino County carry some of the strictest timelines and evidence requirements in California civil law. If you or a family member suffered harm from a delayed diagnosis, a surgical error, or a medication mistake at a Highland clinic or a nearby hospital, the law generally gives you one year from when you discovered the harm, and no more than three years from the date of injury, to act. Before any lawsuit can even be filed, California requires a 90-day written notice to the provider. Because these claims almost always need a qualified medical expert to establish that the care fell below an accepted standard, having someone review your file early matters. LawProactive doesn't practice law or handle your claim directly — we simply connect you with an independent attorney in our network who can evaluate whether your situation involves a compensable error, free of charge and with no obligation.

whyChoose.title: Why Understanding MICRA Matters in Highland

items.title: Strict Filing Deadlines
items.desc: California generally requires medical malpractice claims to be filed within one year of discovering the harm, and no later than three years from the injury itself. Missing this window can end a claim before it starts.

items.title: Mandatory 90-Day Notice
items.desc: Before filing suit, California law requires sending the healthcare provider a 90-day written notice. An attorney can help make sure this step is handled correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Requirement
items.desc: Because a bad medical outcome alone doesn't prove malpractice, these cases typically require a qualified medical expert to show the care fell below an accepted standard. Connecting with an attorney early helps get that review started.

items.question: How long do I have to file a medical malpractice claim in Highland?
items.answer: Under California's MICRA rules, you generally have one year from when you discover the injury, and no more than three years from the date it occurred, to bring a claim. There's also a required 90-day notice to the provider before filing suit. An attorney can help calculate your specific deadline.

items.question: Does a bad medical outcome automatically mean malpractice happened?
items.answer: No. California law requires showing that a provider's care fell below the accepted medical standard, not just that the result was disappointing or unexpected. This usually requires a qualified medical expert to review the records and offer an opinion.

items.question: Are there limits on what I can recover in a California malpractice case?
items.answer: Yes, California law caps non-economic damages in medical malpractice cases, though that cap rises each year under MICRA. Economic damages like medical bills and lost income are generally not subject to this cap. An independent attorney can explain how this may apply to your situation.

items.question: Why does Highland's medical malpractice picture matter locally?
items.answer: Highland residents rely on a mix of local clinics and nearby San Bernardino County hospitals for care, and claims involving these providers still fall under the same statewide MICRA deadlines and notice rules. Getting a records review started early is especially important given how quickly the one-year discovery clock can run.
